interests.name: AI in higher education
interests.description: How AI changes university teaching, tutoring and assessment.

interests.name: Context management in AI

interests.name: Human-AI interaction

candidate.title: Semester-Long Memory for Course Assistants
candidate.abstract: Course assistants built on LLMs forget each student between sessions. We give an assistant a per-student memory that it summarises after every session and retrieves at the start of the next, and deploy it in two introductory programming courses (n = 412) for a full semester. Compared with a stateless assistant, the memory assistant resolved 18% more follow-up questions without a TA, and students rated its answers as more relevant to their own code. Students also reported discomfort when the assistant recalled past mistakes unprompted.

ranking.why: A semester-long deployment of per-student memory in university courses, at the meeting point of both Interests.

picks.fullText: Semester-Long Memory for Course Assistants. 1 Introduction. LLM course assistants answer each question as if meeting the student for the first time. 3 Method. After each session the assistant writes a 200-word summary of the student's goals, misconceptions and code; at the next session it retrieves the three most recent summaries. 5 Results. Over 15 weeks, 412 students in two CS1 sections held 9,870 sessions. Follow-up questions resolved without a TA rose from 61% to 79% (+18 points). Relevance ratings rose from 3.4 to 4.1 of 5. 6 Discussion. 23% of interviewed students said recalled mistakes felt like surveillance; we recommend letting students view and delete their memory.

candidate.title: Compress, Then Forget: Budgeted Context for Long-Horizon Agents
candidate.abstract: Long-horizon agents exceed their context windows and either truncate or summarise. We frame context management as a budgeted selection problem and train a small scorer that decides, every ten steps, which observations to keep verbatim, which to compress and which to drop. On three web and coding agent benchmarks the scorer matches full-context accuracy at 35% of the tokens and beats recursive summarisation by 6 to 11 points.

ranking.why: A learned policy for what an agent keeps, compresses or drops, measured against summarisation.

candidate.title: When Students Overrule the Grader: Contesting AI Feedback on Essays
candidate.abstract: Universities increasingly return AI-generated feedback on written assignments. We built a contest button into an essay feedback tool used by 1,130 undergraduates and analysed 2,604 contests. Students contested 14% of comments; instructors upheld 58% of contests, mostly where the AI misread disciplinary conventions. Students who contested at least once revised more of their essays afterwards than those who never did.

ranking.why: How university students push back on AI feedback, and what instructors make of it.

candidate.title: Trust Calibration Cues in Code Assistants
candidate.abstract: Programmers over-accept wrong suggestions from code assistants. In a controlled study with 96 professional developers, we compare three cues shown next to each suggestion: a confidence score, a highlight of tokens the model was unsure about, and a one-line rationale. Token highlights cut acceptance of wrong suggestions by 27% without slowing developers down; confidence scores had no effect.

ranking.why: A controlled comparison of cues that help people judge when to trust an AI suggestion.

candidate.title: Retrieval Over Lecture Transcripts Beats Longer Context for Course Q&A
candidate.abstract: Should a course question-answering assistant read the whole semester's lecture transcripts in a long context window, or retrieve passages? Across 3 university courses and 1,800 student questions, retrieval of 8 passages answered 9 points more questions correctly than a 1M-token context holding every transcript, at a fiftieth of the cost. Long context did better only on questions spanning several lectures.

ranking.why: Long context against retrieval for a university course assistant, with cost.

picks.fullText: Retrieval Over Lecture Transcripts Beats Longer Context for Course Q&A. 2 Setup. Three courses (statistics, organic chemistry, macroeconomics) recorded 96 lectures. Students asked 1,800 questions through the course forum, each graded by a TA. 4 Results. Retrieval of 8 passages: 71% correct; 1M-token context: 62% correct; cost per question $0.004 against $0.21. On the 140 questions that spanned three or more lectures, long context led by 12 points.

candidate.title: Hint Timing in Step-Based Algebra Tutors: A Classroom Replication
candidate.abstract: Step-based tutors give hints either on request or after an error. We replicate a lab study of hint timing in eight middle-school algebra classrooms (n = 236) over six weeks. Students who received a hint immediately after their second error on a step finished 11% more problems than those who could only request hints, but showed no difference on a delayed post-test. Students who requested hints least benefited most from the immediate hints.

ranking.why: A middle-school tutoring study, outside the Interests.
